references.text: Levi held a great banquet for Jesus, and many tax collectors and others were sitting at the table with them. The Pharisees and the scribes complained that Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners, and Jesus answered that he had come to call sinners to repentance. This is a direct parallel to the situation in [ref:Luk 5:29-32|Luke 5:29-32], where tax collectors and sinners gathered around Jesus.

Jesus describes himself as one who has come and "eats and drinks", and people call him "a friend of tax collectors and sinners" ([ref:Luk 7:34|Luke 7:34]). This confirms the pattern in Luke 15:1 where tax collectors and sinners sought his company.

When Jesus entered Zacchaeus' house, the people grumbled and said: "He has gone to be the guest of a sinful man." ([ref:Luk 19:7|Luke 19:7]). This shows the same reaction pattern as in Luke 15:1-2, where tax collectors and sinners came near Jesus and the religious leaders complained.

In [ref:Matt 9:10-13|Matthew 9:10-13], Jesus is sitting at the table with many tax collectors and sinners, and the Pharisees ask his disciples why their teacher eats with tax collectors and sinners. Jesus answers by quoting Hosea 6:6 and says he has come to call sinners. A parallel to the situation in Luke 15:1.

In [ref:Mark 2:15-17|Mark 2:15-17], Jesus eats with tax collectors and sinners at Levi's house, and the scribes among the Pharisees react. Jesus answers that it is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. A clear parallel to Luke 15:1.
In [ref:Matt 11:19|Matthew 11:19], Jesus is called "a friend of tax collectors and sinners" – a description that mirrors Luke 15:1 where tax collectors and sinners came to him to hear him.

In [ref:Esek 34:11-16|Ezekiel 34:11-16], the Lord himself promises to search for his sheep, gather them, and care for the lost and the injured. This Old Testament background sheds light on why Jesus, as the good shepherd, welcomes sinners and tax collectors as described in Luke 15:1.

[ref:Luk 15:2|Luke 15:2] gives the immediate context: the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled and said "This man welcomes sinners and eats with them." The grumbling is a direct response to tax collectors and sinners coming near Jesus in verse 1.

In [ref:Matt 21:31-32|Matthew 21:31-32], Jesus says that tax collectors and prostitutes are entering the kingdom of God ahead of the Pharisees, because they believed when John came. This shows the same theme: the despised sinners responded positively to God's message, just as the tax collectors and sinners in Luke 15:1 came to hear Jesus.
